name: Spartan communism and the abolition of private wealth
plain_explanation: Sparta forbade gold and silver money, gave every citizen an equal, non-saleable plot of land worked by helots, and required communal dining, in order to prevent both poverty and excessive riches.
precise_definition: The Lycurgan economic arrangement, as reported by Plutarch: equal land allotments ('lots') assigned by the state and worked by helot serfs, an iron-only currency of negligible value, and compulsory communal messes, intended to abolish class division among citizens.
why_it_mattered: It is the direct institutional model Russell says lies behind Plato's proposal, in the Republic, that the guardian class hold no private property.
historical_origin: Attributed by legend to the (probably mythical) lawgiver Lycurgus.
examples: Iron coinage so bulky that ten minas' worth would fill a cellar.
Every citizen dining in a common mess, contributing produce from his lot.
objections: Aristotle notes the system did not actually prevent inequality: two-fifths of all land belonged to women, and lots could be given or bequeathed, leading to a drastic decline in the number of citizens (from about ten thousand to under one thousand by the time of Leuctra).
influence_on_later_thinkers: Prefigures the communism of property Plato proposes for the guardian class in the Republic.
